catalog_locator: Sect. 2.1 'Syllables and “feet”', printed p. 2 (PDF p. 3); sect. 2.1.1 'Reduction and reinterpretation', printed pp. 2-3 (PDF pp. 3-4); sect. 2.3 'Verb suffixes', p. 4 (PDF p. 5); sect. 3.1.3, p. 8 (PDF p. 9); sect. 3.2.2.2, p. 12 (PDF p. 13); sect. 3.4.1 'Basic tones', p. 19 (PDF p. 20). printed page = PDF page - 1).
catalog_quote: Minor feet always have a CV syllable structure. They do not exhibit contrastive length or stress, nor do they contain reduced segmentals. Minor feet that follow a major foot will be shorter and less stressed in absolute terms than are minor feet that precede a major foot. Major feet, when present, are usually the parts of a word that carry the greatest stress, and can have CVV, CVʔV, CVCrVr, or CVrCrV syllable structure, where Vr and Cr stand for reduced vowel and reduced consonant respectively. ... Most words have only one major foot. ... Despite these tendencies in the language, there are a number of words composed solely of minor feet. Examples include: /pe/ “ready”, /tɔgɔ/ “earthworm”, and /cogolo/ “graspings”. In such words, the primary stress falls on the initial foot. All feet in these instances are of roughly the same duration.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: text layer present, extracted text used, no scanned). Page numbers sit at the top-right of each page, so printed p. N = PDF p. N+1, exactly as the reader's locator states. Every clause of the quoted passage is present verbatim: "Minor feet always have a CV syllable structure. They do not exhibit contrastive length or stress, nor do they contain reduced segmentals. Minor feet that follow a major foot will be shorter and less stressed in absolute terms than are minor feet that precede a major foot." and "Major feet, when present, are usually the parts of a word that carry the greatest stress, and can have CVV, CVʔV, CVCrVr, or CVrCrV syllable structure" (sect. 2.1, printed p. 2 = PDF p. 3); "…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nyarafolo is a three-tone language (H, M, L). Word prominence ('stress') is not contrastive: it goes to the word's major foot, i.e. the heavy foot (CVV, CVʔV, or a foot containing reduced segments CVCrVr/CVrCrV), and most words have exactly one such foot. Light CV ('minor') feet are unstressed; in words made only of light feet the primary stress falls on the initial foot. Noun-class suffixes and grammatical morphemes sit in the position of least stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such. The source notes a gradient: minor feet following a major foot are shorter and less stressed than minor feet preceding it, and grammatical morphemes/class suffixes receive least stress.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Most' words have one major foot and major feet 'usually' carry the greatest stress, so words with two major feet (compounds) are left open; vowel-length/stress in initial reduced [a] syllables is stated to be unclear (sect. 3.2.2.2, p. 12). Data are from the Kakpuʔɔrɔ dialect; the author says other dialects vary.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms elicited from four speakers; feet are word-internal units. The 'stress' is an impressionistic duration/prominence notion in a tone language (the alternative reading 'tone language with a stress statement' also applies). Draft working paper 'posted as is without peer review'.
new_statements.identity_note: DeGraaf 2022 describes the Kakpuʔɔrɔ (Kakpuhɔrɔ) variety of Nyarafolo spoken in Ferkessédougou prefecture, 'generally judged to be the most prestigious and widely understood' of the five main dialects the speakers recognise; Glottolog nyar1245 has no dialect children, so this is the language-level entry (ISO sev). The Conseibo 1996 thesis concerns the Nambonkaha dialect.

Describes the Kakpuʔɔrɔ dialect.
